_: One suffix, one meaning, across every semantic token family.
config/prop-vocabulary.json does this for component PROPS and has since
2026-08. Tokens had no equivalent, and the cost showed: `-emphasis` read as a
synonym of the base because in the LIGHT theme it resolves to the same value,
and only the dark theme reveals it as a separate role (2026-08-26). A word
whose meaning you can only recover by reading three theme blocks is a word
nobody can use correctly.
The model is the one the field converged on: a name reads namespace -> object
-> base -> modifier, modifiers last, one ordering for the whole system
(Nathan Curtis / EightShapes). Prominence is ONE ordered axis and interaction
state is a small closed set (Atlassian). The W3C DTCG format we export
standardises the FILE, not the names, so the names are ours to hold.
scripts/lint-token-vocab.mjs fails on a suffix that is not declared here.
It also holds the ALIASES: a semantic token whose value is another semantic
token rather than a primitive. They are legitimate — a chart axis IS label
text, and spelling the primitive twice would mean changing it twice — but they
are the one place in the token layer where editing one role silently moves
another, and until 2026-08-26 nothing checked them. Each is declared below with
the role it follows, so the coupling is a decision someone made rather than a
line someone copied. `diverges` names the themes where the alias deliberately
does NOT hold, which is the case a reader would otherwise call a bug.

foreground.axis: what is written ON this role
foreground.means: the ink that sits on the role's own fill. `--success-foreground` is the ink on a solid success fill, never the colour of success itself.

soft.axis: the same role as a pale wash
soft.means: the subtle end of the prominence axis: a tinted background a dark text can sit on. Pairs with `-soft-foreground`.
soft.why: This and the base form the two steps every status family has: soft = subtle, base = bold. The industry names them subtle/bold; this system named them first and the pair is coherent, so the words stay.

soft-foreground.axis: what is written on the pale wash
soft-foreground.means: the ink for `-soft`. Two foregrounds per family because the two fills need opposite inks.

border.means: the hairline around a soft fill, and nothing else.

emphasis.axis: the role as a MARK, not as a fill
emphasis.means: the status when it must be drawn rather than filled: an icon, a spark, a bar, a dot. It lightens in dark while the fill does not, which is the whole reason it exists.
emphasis.why: In the light theme it resolves to the same value as the base for destructive and success, which makes it look like a duplicate. It is not: in dark the fill stays danger-800 and this goes danger-300. Deleting it would have broken dark mode in six products (caught 2026-08-26 before the delete).

strong.axis: one step further from the surface
strong.means: a quiet neutral made more visible: `--accent-strong`, `--border-strong`. Not a status, not the brand.

hover.means: matches the `:hover` selector that reads it.

active.means: matches the `:active` selector that reads it. `pressed` was used once and renamed on 2026-08-26: one state, one word.

quiet.axis: the same role, said softly, as INK
quiet.means: a link that does not shout. `-soft` is a fill, this is ink.

muted.axis: the neutral grey of a thing
muted.means: `--icon-muted`, `--muted-foreground`. The system's grey, not a dimmed version of a role.

accent.means: `--primary-accent` is the brand colour itself, where `--primary` may be tuned for a fill.

--link.why: a link is the brand speaking in running text; it is the accent, not a colour that resembles it.

--link-hover.why: in light, hovering a link deepens it the way hovering the brand deepens it.
--link-hover.divergence: dark cannot go deeper — it goes LIGHTER (--brand-100), so the dark theme sets its own value. This is the pair the -emphasis near-miss was about: identical in light, opposite in dark.

--link-quiet.why: a link that is not the point of the sentence carries the weight of secondary text.

--chart-grid.why: a gridline is a border drawn inside the plot; it separates without being read.

--chart-axis.why: axis labels ARE secondary text. If secondary text gets lighter, so must they, or the chart stops matching the page around it.

--chart-track.why: the unfilled part of a bar is the same quiet ground a hovered row sits on.

--surface-contrast.why: a control that has to read on ANY surface stands on the card colour, because that is the surface the system guarantees contrast against.

--surface-contrast-hover.why: hovering that control is the same step as hovering anything else on a card.

--surface-contrast-active.why: pressing it is the next step on the same ladder.

--nav-active.why: the current place is marked by the brand's own pale wash, not by a grey. It followed --muted until 2026-08-30, and a quiet ground is exactly what hover already spends: the two states said the same thing, and on a collapsed icon rail the current item stopped reading at all.

--nav-active-border.why: the hairline around the current place is the same brand ink its label is written in. On a 40px disc the tint alone has no room to carry the message; the edge is what makes it unmistakable.

--nav-active-foreground.why: the label of the current page is the brand, the same brand a link is. It spelled --brand-200 in the dark theme until 2026-08-26 — the same value, reached by hand, which would have stayed behind the day the brand moved.
